notes:
I could only use some sources. The commentary pages I read in full were Enduring Word (David Guzik), Precept Austin, and bible.org's Exegetical Commentary on John 5. Everything else comes from search-result excerpts. The Enduring Word page cut off at v. 16, so I have little from Guzik on vv. 17–24. I found nothing from wesley.nnu.edu, seedbed.com, the Lutheran sites (lcms.org, 1517.org), ag.org or pneumareview.com, so those voices are missing. The one Methodist voice is Adam Clarke's commentary on StudyLight.

## Verse-by-verse notes

**v. 1**
- John doesn't say which feast this was. It was probably one of the three feasts every Jewish man had to attend. The debate is between Passover, Pentecost and Purim; if it was a Passover, Jesus' ministry lasted about 3½ years. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-5/
- The NET note (quoted on Precept Austin) prefers the reading "a feast," without "the." That points away from Passover, and so does the fact that the sick were lying outdoors, since Passover fell in the cold late winter. https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-5-commentary
- The NET note tentatively suggests Pentecost, which Jewish tradition linked with Moses receiving the Law; that might explain the mention of Moses in vv. 45–46. Its main point is that the day being a Sabbath is what matters. https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-5-commentary
- Spurgeon says Jesus went because He respected the Law, and because a feast gave Him large crowds to preach to. https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-5-commentary
- J. Vernon McGee calls this miracle the turning point of Jesus' ministry, because it started the hostility that ended at the cross. https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-5-commentary

**v. 2**
- The pool has been excavated just north of the temple area, and it did have five porches, as John says. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-5/
- bible.org identifies the site as the double pool of St. Anne. It had colonnades on all four sides plus one along the middle wall, making five. https://bible.org/seriespage/8-exegetical-commentary-john-5
- Clarke (Methodist) says the name means "house of mercy," probably because of the healings God did there. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/john-5.html
- Another source says a Qumran scroll gives the name, meaning "house of mercy" or "house of double spring." https://bible.org/book/export/html/19298
- Gill (Baptist) uses the pool as a picture of preaching and the church: a "house of mercy" where God's grace is announced. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/5-2.html

**v. 3**
- Many sick people gathered hoping to be healed. Guzik says that hope may have been real, or it may have been only a hopeful legend. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-5/
- Spurgeon notes that none of the crowd looked to Jesus: their eyes were fixed on the water. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-5/

**v. 4 (the disputed verse)**
- *Manuscripts:*
  - Constable says the passage is doubtful, since no Greek manuscript before AD 400 has it. He thinks scribes added it to explain the stirring mentioned in v. 7. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/5-4.html
  - Bratcher (quoted on Precept Austin) thinks it began as a scribe's note in the margin explaining the gathering. https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-5-commentary
  - Trench (quoted by Guzik) calls it a very early insertion, known at least as early as Tertullian in the 2nd century. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-5/
  - Coffman accepts that it was rightly removed, but is glad it stays in the margin because it explains the popular belief. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/john-5.html
- *A minority scholarly view:* the bible.org commentary leans toward keeping some of it. It argues that v. 7 is unclear without it, and that John usually explains Jewish customs for his readers. https://bible.org/seriespage/8-exegetical-commentary-john-5
- *Was the angel real?*
  - Matthew Henry dismisses natural explanations as groundless. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jhn/Jhn_005.cfm
  - Clarke calls such theories "a miserable shift" to explain away God's power. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/john-5.html
  - Barnes (Presbyterian), by contrast, thinks the water had medicinal properties and probably healed gradually. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/5-4.htm
- *Charismatic / popular teaching:*
  - Chuck Smith (Calvary Chapel) treats the stirred water as a "point of contact" that turns faith from passive to active, like the moment hands are laid on someone in prayer. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/5-4.html
  - Everett's Study Notes repeat Todd Bentley's claim that the Lord told him He is "releasing the pools of Bethesda" across the world. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghe/john-5.html
  - Guzik offers a caution: God does act in unexpected ways, but something isn't from God just because it is unusual. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-5/

**v. 5**
- The man's hope had been disappointed for 38 years. Out of a whole crowd, Jesus chose this one man; He wasn't holding a healing crusade. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-5/
- Guzik describes, without endorsing, an old allegory: the man is Israel, the five porches are the Law, the 38 years echo the wilderness wanderings, and the water is baptism. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/archives/guzik_david/StudyGuide_Jhn/Jhn_5.cfm

**v. 6**
- The bible.org commentary thinks John means Jesus knew the man's history supernaturally. https://bible.org/seriespage/8-exegetical-commentary-john-5
- Guzik calls "Do you want to get well?" a sincere question. Some sick people lose hope, and a beggar could lose his living if healed (Barclay). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-5/

**v. 7**
- Calvin (quoted by Guzik) says the man limits God's help to what he can imagine. Guzik sees him as a mix of hope and hopelessness. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-5/

**vv. 8–9**
- Jesus told the man to do what he couldn't do, and the healing came as he obeyed in faith. Dods says carrying the mat showed the cure was permanent. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-5/
- Trench says Jesus healed without the water to show He didn't need it. Guzik then lists several ways the New Testament says people may be healed: anointing by elders, laying on of hands, gifts of healing, faith, and medicine. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-5/
- bible.org notes that the Sabbath detail is what sets off the conflict. https://bible.org/seriespage/8-exegetical-commentary-john-5

**v. 10**
- In John, "the Jews" usually means the religious leaders in Jerusalem (Bruce). Carrying the mat broke the rabbis' interpretation of the Sabbath, not God's own law. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-5/
- Precept Austin, citing Kruse, warns readers not to take "the Jews" in an anti-Semitic way. https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-5-commentary

**vv. 11–13**
- The leaders weren't interested in who healed him, only in who told him to carry the mat. To them Jesus was a Sabbath-breaker; to the man He was the one who made him well. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-5/
- Alford says Jesus slipped into the crowd so as not to draw attention, since He didn't intend to heal everyone there. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-5/

**v. 14 (does sin cause sickness?)**
- Jesus sought the man out because He cared about his soul: a sinful life is worse than 38 years of paralysis. Maclaren thinks this illness came from a sin of the flesh. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-5/
- Barnes says the words imply the illness came from sin, perhaps vice in his youth. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/ubv/john/5-14.html
- Clarke says Jesus showed He knew both the man's past sins and his future danger. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/asv/john/5-14.html
- Gill says "something worse" could be a worse illness or punishment in this life or the next. For a true believer, he says, it could be God hiding His face. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/ubv/john/5-14.html
- bible.org adds balance. In John 9:3 Jesus denies that sickness always comes from sin, and here "something worse" probably means the final judgment (compare v. 29), not a worse illness. https://bible.org/seriespage/8-exegetical-commentary-john-5

**v. 15**
- Morris thinks the man was an unpleasant character who betrayed his healer. Guzik says it shows how intimidated he was. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-5/
- Raymond Brown (quoted on bible.org) sees naivety rather than treachery here. https://bible.org/seriespage/8-exegetical-commentary-john-5

**v. 16**
- The plural "these things" suggests Jesus healed on the Sabbath more than once, and John chose this case as an example. https://bible.org/seriespage/8-exegetical-commentary-john-5
- Bruce says encouraging others to break the law was seen as worse than breaking it yourself, and the leaders' campaign didn't let up until His death. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-5/

**v. 17**
- Even the rabbis granted that God keeps working on the Sabbath: babies are born and people die on it. Jesus claimed that same right, which was claiming a privilege that belongs to God alone. https://bible.org/seriespage/8-exegetical-commentary-john-5
- Jesus said "My Father," not "your" or "our" Father. https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-5-commentary

**v. 18**
- The leaders understood clearly that Jesus was claiming to be equal with God. Morris notes the verbs describe ongoing action: Jesus habitually broke their rules and habitually made the claim. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-5/
- Matthew Henry: "the Jews understand what the Arians do not" (the Arians denied that Christ is fully God). He adds that it would have been a terrible crime if Jesus were not in fact equal with God. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jhn/Jhn_005.cfm
- Clarke says the leaders read Jesus correctly: He and the Father are one. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/john-5.html
- Guzik: Jesus claimed equality with the Father, not to be the same person as the Father. https://blueletterbible.org/Comm/guzik_david/StudyGuide_Jhn/Jhn_5.cfm

**v. 19**
- Jesus depends completely on the Father. Father and Son share one essence and act as one. https://bible.org/seriespage/8-exegetical-commentary-john-5

**vv. 20–23**
- The works the Son does are the same works the rabbis accepted God doing on the Sabbath: giving life and judging. The Father gives physical life, while the Son gives spiritual life (the "greater works"). https://bible.org/seriespage/8-exegetical-commentary-john-5
- Matthew Henry says the honour due to the Son is honour no creature could rightly receive. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jhn/Jhn_005.cfm

**v. 24 (can eternal life be lost?)**
- *What it means:*
  - Gill: the believer passes from spiritual death to life and from condemnation to justification, and is safe from the "second death." https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/kjv/john/5-24.html
  - Clarke: the seed of this life is planted the moment a person believes. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nlt/john/5-24.html
  - bible.org: eternal life is something believers have now, though John also looks ahead to the final judgment in vv. 28–29. https://bible.org/seriespage/8-exegetical-commentary-john-5
- *Reformed:* The Gospel Coalition sees a permanent move from death to life. All true believers will persevere, and good works are the evidence. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/essay/preservation-and-perseverance/
- *Evangelical:* GotQuestions says believers are eternally secure because of Christ's finished work. https://www.gotquestions.org/passed-from-death-to-life.html
- *Catholic:* Catholic Answers argues the verse doesn't teach "once saved, always saved." Belief is the condition, belief can be lost, and losing it means losing the life. https://www.catholic.com/audio/drk/eternal-life-means-forever-saved-right
- I found no Wesleyan, Lutheran or Pentecostal source on this verse, so their positions aren't covered.

## Catholic and Orthodox readings (vv. 2–4)
- Chrysostom reads the pool as a picture of baptism. It wasn't the water alone that healed but the angel's action; in the same way, baptism works when the Spirit's grace is joined to it. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/240136.htm
- Matthew Henry (Protestant) makes a similar link: baptism is like the pool, but open at all times, not just at certain seasons. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jhn/Jhn_005.cfm
- Fr. Lawrence Farley (OCA) compares the man's long wait to Israel waiting for salvation. The angel stirring the water recalls the Law given through angels, and the five porches match the five books of Moses, a point he credits to Augustine. https://www.oca.org/reflections/fr.-lawrence-farley/the-paralytic-and-the-pool
